claims.quote: Aortic diameter ≥3 cm; rupture → retroperitoneal hematoma Abdominal aortic aneurysm

claims.quote: Curvilinear calcified aortic shadow >3 cm Abdominal aortic aneurysm US screening; CTA if symptomatic; repair ≥5.5 cm

claims.text: Plain radiographs are neither sensitive nor specific, but may show aortic calcification outlining the aneurysm wall
claims.quote: Plain abdominal radiographs are neither sensitive nor specific; however, if obtained for other purposes, radiographs may show aortic calcification outlining the aneurysm wall.

claims.text: By definition, an aortic diameter ≥ 3 cm is an AAA; they typically begin below the renal arteries (infrarenal); about 50% involve the iliac arteries; most are fusiform and many are lined with laminated thrombus
claims.quote: AAAs typically begin below the renal arteries (infrarenal) (2) but may include the renal arterial ostia (pararenal); about 50% involve the iliac arteries. By definition, an aortic diameter ≥ 3 cm constitutes an AAA. Most AAAs are fusiform (circumferential widening of the artery). Many are lined with laminated thrombus.

claims.text: Unstable with presumed rupture: bedside ultrasound gives results more rapidly, but intestinal gas and distention may limit its accuracy
claims.quote: For patients who are hemodynamically unstable with presumed rupture, ultrasound provides bedside results more rapidly, but intestinal gas and distention may limit its accuracy.

claims.text: If rupture is not suspected, CTA or MRA can more precisely characterize aneurysm size and anatomy
claims.quote: If rupture is not suspected, CT angiography (CTA) or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) can more precisely characterize aneurysm size and anatomy.

claims.text: Causes Multifactorial; commonly a weakening of the arterial wall, usually by atherosclerosis; also trauma, cystic medial necrosis, anastomotic disruption, vasculitis; mycotic aneurysms (S. aureus, then Salmonella)
claims.quote: Etiology of abdominal aortic aneurysms is multifactorial but commonly involves a weakening of the arterial wall, usually by Atherosclerosis Other causes include Trauma Cystic medial necrosis (degeneration of the aortic media) Postsurgical anastomotic disruption Vasculitis (eg, Takayasu arteritis) Uncommonly, syphilis and localized bacterial or fungal infection, typically due to sepsis or infective endocarditis, weaken the arterial wall and cause infected (mycotic) aneurysms. Staphylococcus aureus is the number one cause of mycotic aneurysms, followed by Salmonella.

claims.text: Risk factors: smoking (strongest), hypertension, older age (peak 70 to 80 years), family history, White race, male sex, inherited connective tissue disorders
claims.quote: Risk factors for abdominal aortic aneurysms include Smoking (strongest risk factor) Hypertension Older age (peak incidence at age 70 to 80 years) Family history (in 15 to 25%) Race (more common among White patients than among patients with African ancestry) Male sex Inherited connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome)

claims.text: Symptoms Most are asymptomatic; expansion may cause steady, deep, boring lumbosacral pain; patients may notice a prominent abdominal pulsation; rapidly enlarging aneurysms about to rupture can be tender
claims.quote: Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are asymptomatic. Symptoms and signs, when they do occur, may be nonspecific but usually result from compression of adjacent structures. As AAAs expand, they may cause pain, which is steady, deep, boring, visceral, and felt most prominently in the lumbosacral region. Patients may be aware of an abnormally prominent abdominal pulsation. Although most aneurysms grow slowly, rapidly enlarging aneurysms that are about to rupture can be tender.

claims.text: Rupture: most die before reaching care; survivors typically have abdominal or back pain, hypotension and tachycardia
claims.quote: If an AAA ruptures, most patients die before reaching a medical facility. Patients who do not die immediately typically present with abdominal or back pain, hypotension, and tachycardia.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: repair if ≥5.5 cm, growth >0.5 cm/6 mo, or symptomatic
claims.quote: Repair if ≥5.5 cm, growth >0.5 cm/6 mo, or symptomatic

claims.text: Elective repair for aneurysms > 5 cm in females and > 5.5 cm in males, rapidly enlarging ones, or those causing ischemic or embolic complications
claims.quote: Elective surgical repair is recommended for aneurysms > 5 cm in females, for those > 5.5 cm in males, and for those that are rapidly enlarging or causing ischemic or embolic complications.

claims.text: Also an indication: growth > 0.5 cm within 6 months, regardless of size; chronic abdominal pain; > 4.5 cm with Marfan syndrome
claims.quote: Additional indications for elective surgery include Increase in aneurysm size by > 0.5 cm within 6 months, regardless of size Chronic abdominal pain Thromboembolic complications Iliac or femoral artery aneurysm that causes lower-limb ischemia Aneurysms > 4.5 cm in patients with Marfan syndrome

claims.text: Ruptured AAA: immediate open surgery or endovascular stent grafting; without treatment, mortality approaches 100%
claims.quote: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysms require immediate open surgery or endovascular stent grafting. Without treatment, mortality rate approaches 100%.

claims.text: In hemorrhagic shock, give fluids and blood but keep MAP no higher than 70 to 80 mm Hg (permissive hypotension), because bleeding may increase
claims.quote: Patients who present in hemorrhagic shock require fluid resuscitation and blood transfusions, but mean arterial pressure should not be elevated to > 70 to 80 mm Hg (permissive hypotension) because bleeding may increase.

claims.text: In most cases, repairing aneurysms < 5 cm does not appear to increase survival; monitor with ultrasound or abdominal CT every 6 to 12 months for expansion that warrants treatment
claims.quote: In most cases, repair of aneurysms < 5 cm does not appear to increase survival. Aneurysms should be monitored with ultrasound or abdominal CT scans every 6 to 12 months for expansion that warrants treatment.
